library(tidyverse)

# Consistent look for every static plot
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
            theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
                  panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))

panderOptions("table.split.table", Inf)
panderOptions("round", 4)
Code
# Altered an Applr function to graph two line logistic models 
scatter_3d_logistic_two_line <- function(model, n = 50, colors = c("red","blue")) {
  if (!inherits(model, "glm")) stop("Model must be a glm (logistic) model")
  
  vars <- all.vars(formula(model))
  predictors <- vars[-1]  # exclude outcome
  y_name <- vars[1]
  
  if (length(predictors) > 3) stop("Model has too many predictors. Only 2 continuous + 1 factor allowed")
  
  # Detect factor variable among predictors using model$xlevels
  factor_var <- NULL
  continuous_vars <- c()
  for (v in predictors) {
    if (!is.null(model$xlevels[[v]])) {
      factor_var <- v
    } else {
      continuous_vars <- c(continuous_vars, v)
    }
  }
  
  if (length(continuous_vars) != 2) stop("Need exactly 2 continuous predictors for 3D plot")
  x_name <- continuous_vars[1]
  y2_name <- continuous_vars[2]
  
  # Scatter points
  df_plot <- model$model[, c(y_name, x_name, y2_name)]
  if (!is.null(factor_var) && factor_var %in% names(model$model)) {
    df_plot[[factor_var]] <- model$model[[factor_var]]  # keep factor
    levels_factor <- levels(model$model[[factor_var]])
    if (is.null(colors)) colors <- brewer.pal(length(levels_factor), "Set1")
  }
  
  # Rename for plotting
  df_plot2 <- df_plot %>%
    rename(X = !!sym(x_name), Y = !!sym(y2_name), Z = !!sym(y_name))
  
  if (!is.null(factor_var) && factor_var %in% names(df_plot2)) {
    df_plot2[[factor_var]] <- df_plot[[factor_var]]
  }
  
  axisx <- seq(min(df_plot2$X), max(df_plot2$X), length.out = n)
  axisy <- seq(min(df_plot2$Y), max(df_plot2$Y), length.out = n)
  
  # Scatter points
  p <- plot_ly(data = df_plot2, x = ~X, y = ~Y, z = ~Z,
               type = 'scatter3d', mode = 'markers', color = I("black"))
  
  # Add surface(s)
  if (!is.null(factor_var) && factor_var %in% names(df_plot2)) {
    for (i in seq_along(levels_factor)) {
      level <- levels_factor[i]
      
      # Surface grid with original variable names
      surface_df <- setNames(expand.grid(axisx, axisy), c(x_name, y2_name))
      surface_df[[factor_var]] <- factor(level, levels = model$xlevels[[factor_var]])
      
      # Predict probabilities
      surface_df$Z <- predict(model, newdata = surface_df, type = "response")
      
      # Convert to matrix for surface
      Z_matrix <- matrix(surface_df$Z, nrow = length(axisy), ncol = length(axisx), byrow = TRUE)
      
      # Add surface with unique color
      p <- p %>% add_surface(x = axisx, y = axisy, z = Z_matrix,
                             opacity = 0.6,
                             showscale = FALSE,
                             name = paste(factor_var, "=", level),
                             surfacecolor = matrix(rep(i, length(axisx)*length(axisy)), nrow=length(axisy)),
                             colorscale = list(c(0,1), c(colors[i], colors[i])))
    }
  } else {
    # Single surface if no factor
    surface_df <- setNames(expand.grid(axisx, axisy), c(x_name, y2_name))
    surface_df$Z <- predict(model, newdata = surface_df, type = "response")
    Z_matrix <- matrix(surface_df$Z, nrow = length(axisy), ncol = length(axisx), byrow = TRUE)
    
    p <- p %>% add_surface(x = axisx, y = axisy, z = Z_matrix, opacity = 0.6)
  }
  
  # Axis titles
  p <- layout(p, scene = list(
    xaxis = list(title = x_name),
    yaxis = list(title = y2_name),
    zaxis = list(title = y_name)
  ))
  
  p
}

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Predictors Used

Age
Heart failure mortality rises markedly with age. Older patients typically have less physiological reserve and a heavier burden of comorbid conditions, both of which worsen prognosis.

Reduced cardiovascular reserve
Higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease
Lower tolerance for aggressive or advanced therapies



Ejection Fraction
Ejection fraction (EF) is the percentage of blood ejected from the left ventricle with each contraction. A normal EF is approximately 55–70%. A low EF reflects systolic dysfunction and is strongly associated with:

Increased hospitalization rates
Higher risk of ventricular arrhythmias
Elevated mortality risk



Serum Creatinine
Serum creatinine reflects kidney function and is a key prognostic marker in heart failure. Elevated creatinine often signals cardiorenal syndrome, in which reduced cardiac output and elevated venous pressure impair renal perfusion and filtration. Renal dysfunction in heart failure is driven by:

Low forward flow, which reduces renal blood supply
Chronic venous congestion, which increases renal interstitial pressure
Neurohormonal activation (RAAS and sympathetic systems), which worsens both cardiac and renal function

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Source and Preparation
The data come from the UCI Heart Failure Clinical Records dataset, which contains clinical information on 299 patients with heart failure. It includes demographic variables, comorbidities, laboratory measurements, cardiac function indicators, and a binary outcome indicating mortality during follow-up.


Code
# Save as a temp file
temp_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")

url <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/519/heart+failure+clinical+records.zip"
download.file(url, destfile = temp_zip, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)

zip_contents <- unzip(temp_zip, list = TRUE)

temp_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
unzip(temp_zip, files = "heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv", exdir = dirname(temp_csv))

# Read from temp
df <- read_csv(file.path(dirname(temp_csv), "heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv"))




Code
# Create new variable
df$eighty_years_old <- factor(ifelse(df$age >= 80, 1, 0),
                              levels = c(0, 1),
                              labels = c("Under80", "80plus"))








A note on the time variable



The strongest single predictor in the dataset was time, the length of the follow-up period. Using it would be “cheating”: patients who died stopped being observed and therefore have short follow-up times, while survivors were observed for the entire study. We discarded this variable.

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Mathematical Model
Let \(p_i\) be the probability that patient \(i\) dies during follow-up. The model is
\[
\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{EF}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Creatinine}_i + \beta_3\,\text{Age80Plus}_i
\]
or, equivalently, in terms of probability,
\[
P(\text{Mortality}_i = 1 \mid \cdot) =
\frac{e^{\,\beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{EF}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Creatinine}_i + \beta_3\,\text{Age80Plus}_i}}
     {1 + e^{\,\beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{EF}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Creatinine}_i + \beta_3\,\text{Age80Plus}_i}}
\]
where \(\text{Age80Plus}_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) is 80 or older and \(0\) otherwise.

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Fitting the Model
We split the data into a 75% training set and a 25% test set, fit the model on the training data, and evaluate it on the test data.

  rename(
    `Mortality (Death Event)` = DEATH_EVENT,
    `Ejection Fraction (%)` = ejection_fraction,
    `Serum Creatinine (mg/dL)` = serum_creatinine

n <- nrow(df)

keep <- sample(1:n, size = round(0.75 * n))
mytrain <- df[keep, ]

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Interpretation
Coefficients are on the log-odds scale; exponentiating gives odds ratios.

Ejection fraction. Each 1% increase in ejection fraction changes the log-odds of mortality by \(-0.06485\). The odds ratio is \(e^{-0.06485} = 0.94\), so the odds of mortality decrease by about 6% for each additional 1% of blood ejected per contraction.
Serum creatinine. Each 1 mg/dL increase changes the log-odds of mortality by \(0.6664\). The odds ratio is \(e^{0.6664} = 1.95\), so the odds of mortality increase by about 95% for each additional 1 mg/dL of serum creatinine.
Age ≥ 80. Being 80 or older increases the log-odds of mortality by \(1.625\). The odds ratio is \(e^{1.625} = 5.08\), so the odds of mortality increase by about 408% for patients 80 or older.

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
3D Visualization of the Model
The plot shows predicted mortality probability as a function of ejection fraction and serum creatinine. The red plane is for patients under 80 and the blue plane is for patients 80 or older; the gap between them shows the substantially higher predicted risk in the older group. Black points are observed outcomes in the training data.


Code
scatter_3d_logistic_two_line(my_glm)

title: Heart Attack Mortality Logistic Regression
text:
Limitations

The model was evaluated on a single random train/test split of a small dataset (299 patients), so accuracy estimates carry uncertainty.
Dichotomizing age at 80 discards information; a continuous age term may fit better.
Odds ratios describe association, not causation.

title: Paper Airplane ANOVA BF[1]
text:
Study Design

Design Overview
Objective: Determine which of three paper airplane designs (Bomber, Standard, Stone) go the farthest distance when thrown. Further divided by the skill of the thrower (Me and my Wife)
Population: 15 Paper Airplanes
Response Variable: Distance in feet
Treatment Factor: Folding Design / Thrower
Experimental Unit: Type of Design / Thrower
Observational Unit: Each Paper Airplane

Randomization
We have employed the following Randomizations:
Random Selection of Experimental Units: The sheets of paper used for the experiment were randomly selected from the available paper.
Random Assignment of Units to Treatment: The sheets of paper were randomly assigned to one of the three airplane designs: Bomber, Standard, or Stone. The order in which the planes were folded was also randomized.
Random Order of Experimental Runs: The order in which the completed airplanes were thrown was randomized. This helped prevent factors such as changes in throwing ability or fatigue from favoring one particular design.



Factors

Controlled - Varied

Airplane design
Thrower of teh airplanes



Controlled - Held Constant

Where the planes were thrown (The Hinkley Gym)
Type of Paper (A4 print paper)
Standing position
Folder of the airplanes (Me)



Not Controlled - Measured

None



Not Controlled - Not Measured

Ac cause air movement
Strength of the throw




Types of Planes

The Bomber



Bomber


The Bomber is a plane I made most commonly when I was a child. It is the coolest looking of the three


The Standard



Standard


This is a standard paper airplane that children first learn to make.


The Stone



Stone


This is the plane my dad used to win a paper airplane contest when I was a child. There is considerable discourse on whether or not this qualifies as a plane. I am on the side of the supporters.


All together

All models



All Models


All Paper Airplane models side by side




Hyposthesis
\[
\text{Level of Significance}=0.05
\]

Plane Design
\[
H_0: \alpha_\text{Bomber} = \alpha_\text{Standard} = \alpha_\text{Stone} = 0
\]
\[
H_a: \alpha_\text{At Least One} \neq 0
\]
Our Null Hypothesis states that the design of the plane has no effect on the distance thrown. I.E. that the \(\alpha\) is 0 for each level.
Our Alternative Hypothesis states that at least one design will have a different average distance when thrown than the others.


Thrower
\[
H_0: \beta_\text{Me} = \beta_\text{my wife} = 0
\]
\[
H_a: \beta_\text{Me} \neq \beta_\text{my wife}
\]
Our Null Hypothesis states that the thrower of the plane has no effect on the distance thrown. I.E. that the \(\beta\) is 0 for both levels.
Our Alternative Hypothesis states that one thrower will have a different average distance when thrown than the others.

title: Paper Airplane ANOVA BF[1]
text:
Data Collection
We collected our data by throwing the 15 paper airplanes in an empty gymnasium at the BYUI University as it was the most controlled environment available to us at the time. my wife threw her planes for an earlier experiment (Case Study 1). I threw his at a different time with the same randomizations and experiment structure. We measured how far each plane flew and recorded the data in feet.

title: Predicting Housing Prices with a Two Lines Linear Regression Model
text:
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(pander)

title: Predicting Housing Prices with a Two Lines Linear Regression Model
text:
Model Specification
We fit a linear model in which the effect of square footage is allowed to differ by neighborhood type:
\[
\widehat{\text{SalePrice}}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{TotalSF}_i + \beta_2\,\text{RichNbrhd}_i + \beta_3\,(\text{TotalSF}_i \times \text{RichNbrhd}_i)
\]
where \(\text{RichNbrhd}_i = 1\) for a home in a high-priced neighborhood and \(0\) otherwise. This gives two lines:
\[
\text{Standard } (\text{RichNbrhd}=0):\quad \widehat{\text{SalePrice}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{TotalSF}
\]
\[
\text{Rich } (\text{RichNbrhd}=1):\quad \widehat{\text{SalePrice}} = (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + (\beta_1 + \beta_3)\,\text{TotalSF}
\]
Meaning that \(\beta_2\) is effectively the change in the intercept and \(\beta_3\) is teh change in the slope when a neighborhood is among the rich labelled.
